body.text: Nine parliamentarians will receive security upgrades to their electoral offices after raising concerns in the wake of the alleged attack on Helen Haines last week.

Disruptions 'inevitable' as AI-powered cyber threats grow, spy boss says
Australia's top cyber spy is warning the country to prepare for more frequent disruptions to everyday services amid a surge of AI-powered cyber attacks.
Australian Signals Directorate (ASD) director-general Abigail Bradshaw says artificial intelligence frontier models have "redefined" the threat facing Australia.
"What is inevitable is that with each capability increase, we are likely to see more disruption," she said.
"Disruption can look like what we've seen over the last few weeks, with websites that require patching having to be taken down in order to be secured.
"Disruption could look like data breaches. Disruption could look like service disruption.
"Virtually any service that you rely on in your life today is enabled in some respect by a digital network."
Today the ASD is publishing its annual cyber threat report, which details a 20 per cent jump in cyber security incidents the agency was required to respond to last financial year.
Top official says Senate estimates interrogations a 'health and safety' risk for staff
Australia's most senior public servant says the conduct of some politicians "demeans, intimidates [and] humiliates" officials.

The conduct at Senate estimates and other committees has been a bubbling concern in the public service. Last month, a defence official made waves when she said she didn't want her answers to be clipped up for social media.
And it's those clips Steven Kennedy, secretary of the prime minister's department, had in mind in his own estimates appearance on Monday evening.
He says "misleading" edits shared by politicians "invite ridicule, hostility or abuse directed at individual public servants".
And while he does not propose to censor videos, he asks politicians to remember their obligations to engage courteously and urges them to monitor any social media posts to remove "vile abuse".
First US submarine to be deployed for WA rotational force
The US Navy has identified which of its submarines will be deployed to Australia first for the "rotational force" being established under AUKUS.

AUKUS proponents in Washington say it's proof the US is moving "full steam ahead" on the plan to arm Australia with nuclear-powered submarines, despite the concerns around shortfalls in the US's own fleet.
Fast-attack submarine USS Colorado will be part of Submarine Rotational Force-West (SRF-West) from late next year, the Pentagon says.
The Virginia-class boat will be the first of up to four American submarines to rotate through HMAS Stirling, near Perth, under SRF-West. One British boat is also expected to be part of the rotation.
The rotational force is aimed at helping Australia prepare to operate its own nuclear-powered, conventionally armed submarines down the track.
USS Colorado joined the US Navy fleet in 2018. It is crewed by 134 personnel.

"The activation of SRF-West puts Australia one step closer along the Optimal Pathway to Australia operating its own nuclear-powered submarine capability," said congressman Joe Courtney, who co-chairs Congress's Friends of Australia caucus."The combination of US and UK attack submarine rotations and Australian nuclear-powered submarines will transform allied naval posture in the Indo-Pacific."

"The combination of US and UK attack submarine rotations and Australian nuclear-powered submarines will transform allied naval posture in the Indo-Pacific."
USS Colorado completed a six-month deployment to waters off Europe in December 2023.

The following year, it was moved to Pearl Harbor, Hawaii, for a two-year maintenance period. In June, the US Navy announced its return to its fleet after maintenance finished a month ahead of schedule.
Coalition says aged care algorithm is 'fundamentally flawed'
A Commonwealth Ombudsman warned in a scathing report that the use of automation in the aged care system lacks safeguards and has led to unfair outcomes for elderly patients.
Finance Minister Katy Gallagher defended the government's response, telling ABC's Radio National Breakfast action had been taken to understand the issues with the system.
"We are responding in real time to a new system that's being built, and under enormous pressure from the demand coming our way. There's more work to do there," she says.
Shadow Health Minister Anne Ruston says the system is "fundamentally flawed" and needs a redesign.
"They need to go back to the drawing board and actually have a look, get rid of the algorithm and start again and rebuild it," she says.
Ruston says the opposition doesn't have a problem with technology being used to assist an accessor as a tool but "no computer should ultimately have the decision that should reside with a person".
Savings to be found ahead of MYEFO, Gallagher says
A savings package is being prepared ahead of the mid-year budget update, Finance Minister Katy Gallagher says as high inflation puts pressure on the government to cut spending.

The government has repeatedly blamed the ongoing conflict in the Middle East and AI investment, not spending, as the drivers of inflation. The Reserve Bank is meeting next week to decide whether to lift rates again.

Gallagher tells ABC's Radio National Breakfast it's been hard work to try to convince the parliament to adopt the existing savings identified in the budget — pointing to the debate over the contentious changes to the private health rebate for over 65s.

"We've got a modest save on private health insurance that agree there's a number of people that aren't happy with that. But that's that's about, you know, finding some savings and reinvesting into aged care to deal with the demand we're seeing there," she says."And that's not acceptable to anyone in the Senate at the moment. That just shows you how difficult it is."

'It weighs heavily on people': New AI tool used to help MPs flag violent threats
Almost 5,000 threats and violent comments have been flagged on the social media accounts of 22 Labor politicians in just three months, data from a new AI tool being trailed has found.
Finance Minister Katy Gallagher says the volume, scale and forcefulness of the threats and abusive language is beyond what she's seen in politics before.
She says the AI tool helps reduce some of the pressure on MPs.
"It's just been increasing and it weighs heavily on people," she tells ABC's Radio National Breakfast.
Gallagher says there is currently a discussion underway about formalising a process on how to use the data to inform the federal police.

Asked if there is a concern about censoring genuine robust feedback, Gallagher says she doesn't think so. She says the abusive comments were resulting in well-meaning people not leaving feedback with MPs on social media.
"It's really a work management tool … it's very difficult to go to work every day and just be abused constantly online. So it's about how we manage our working day and that of our staff."
She names Facebook as the worst platform for threats, followed by Instagram and TikTok.
"The platforms have to help us here because, the way it’s going now, our accounts are just a place for people to come and abuse pretty vigorously."
Marles hopeful yesterday wasn't a one-off
The chamber was noticeably subdued across yesterday, including in Question Time, where MPs were on their best behaviour as the parliament paused in support of Helen Haines.
Defence Minister Richard Marles is asked if he thinks MPs will go back to their old ways today.
He tells ABC's News Breakfast that he hopes everyone can do better — including the media.

"I think all of us need to take a responsibility here for the public discourse that we are all a part of. That's where we need to really try and collectively engage in bringing the temperature down and having a much more respectful and civil discourse," he says.
Marles urges organisations to use AI to harden systems against cyber attacks
Australia's cyber-spy agency is warning the country to prepare for disruptions to everyday life, as it deals with a surge in AI-driven cyber attacks.
The Australian Signals Directorate's latest report found a 20 per cent jump in incidents.
Defence Minister Richard Marles attributed this to malicious actors using AI to help them exploit vulnerabilities in systems.

"What we're saying to people right now is if you've got old systems, you've got to get rid of them. If you've got an old system which is connected to the internet, that's a gateway for a malicious actor," he tells ABC's News Breakfast.

"You've got to take time to harden your networks even if that means bringing them down for a couple of days to do that and you need to use AI yourself."There's a lot of AI products out there. Use them."

Key Event
Big mining boss brought in to fix Australia’s Defence buying system
The way Australia buys weapons and defence gear is getting a major overhaul, with former Rio Tinto chief Kellie Parker hired to run the country's new Defence Delivery Agency.

Deputy Prime Minister Richard Marles and Defence Industry Minister Pat Conroy will announce today that Parker will become the new National Armaments Director — effectively making her Australia's chief weapons buyer.

For decades, defence procurement has been bogged down by massive budget blowouts and severe delays. To fix this, the Albanese government is transforming its purchasing division into an independent agency — known as the Defence Delivery Agency — starting July 2027.

By hiring a veteran mining executive accustomed to delivering complex, multi-billion-dollar infrastructure under strict commercial pressures, the government is hoping to inject real-world business discipline into the ADF.
Parker takes on the role in November 2026 before the agency goes fully live in July 2027.
Key Event
NACC holds off on decision over controversial grant scheme inquiry

The NACC says it has not ruled out an investigation into a contentious government grant scheme that saw a golf club in the PM's electorate get $6 million dollars, but is putting any decision on hold until other parliamentary inquiries into the program conclude.

Appearing before Senate estimates, National Anti-Corruption Commission acting commissioner Kylie Kilgour confirmed the agency had received referrals regarding the $560 million Local Community Infrastructure program.
The scheme has faced intense scrutiny after analysis by the Centre for Public Integrity found it heavily favoured Labor electorates.

Kilgour said the scheme had "piqued" her interest but ultimately the watchdog would wait on the outcomes of a parliamentary inquiry and a potential audit by the Australian National Audit Office (ANAO) before taking further action.

"If you've got another integrity agency conducting a process, it's not necessarily appropriate for us to come in," Kilgour noted, adding that the NACC was "not there yet" in determining whether it holds statutory jurisdiction.

During the hearing, Kilgour also paid tribute to independent MP Helen Haines — a prominent critic of the grant scheme and a key architect of the NACC. She remains in hospital after being attacked outside her electorate office last week.
Key Event
Snowy 2.0 boss defends project progress since 2023 reset
Snowy Hydro made a late appearance at yesterday's Senate estimates, where company representatives were grilled over the latest cost blowout for Australia's biggest renewable energy project.
It was revealed last week that the Snowy 2.0 pumped hydro project would cost $22 billion-$25 billion and be delayed another year.

The cost has doubled since a 2023 project reset, where Snowy Hydro and the contractor building the project moved to a revised contract; which includes penalties for poor performance relating to cost and schedule.
Snowy Hydro CEO Dennis Barnes says the increase in cost was mainly due to flaws in the initial design and that there had been significant progress since the new contract model was adopted.
"In 2023, the advice of myself and the Snowy board … was to reset this contract to an ITC model, get progress moving again and we saw progress did double over that period," he said.

Barnes also said the federal government would need to contribute a "substantial proportion" of the extra $10b required to complete the project but that discussions around exactly how much were still underway.
New election funding system ready to go for 2027
The new election funding regime previously had its start date delayed because the Australian Electoral Commission said getting it up and running was a complicated task.
And little wonder: it's a whole new system, with donations to be disclosed in close to real time, and with caps now to apply to candidates, parties and donors.
But in what AEC commissioner Jeff Pope says is a "near miracle", the complicated technical system to make all of that work is now ready to roll from its mooted start date of January 1, 2027.

The next step will be to work with political parties and candidates to make sure they understand how to use the new system. Liberal senator James McGrath, a keen follower of electoral matters, sounds doubtful that it will all be so seamless. But in theory at least, it should be full steam ahead.
Nine politicians to get electorate office security upgrades after Haines attack
The AFP held a security briefing for politicians just two days after the attack on independent MP Helen Haines, and it seems tangible outcomes are already afoot.
Nine electorate offices are now having security concerns actioned after they were raised last week, according to the Department of Finance.
In a late-night Senate estimates hearing, Finance secretary Matt Yannopoulos explains how the system works.
The AFP handles threat assessments and security details, Home Affairs does home security for those eligible, and Finance handles offices and transport. All three co-ordinate and share information.

"Where there's an ask for something to be upgraded, we go about that as quickly as possible, and indeed from the discussions that occurred last week there are nine different offices that are raised and we are dealing with those," Yannopoulos tells the committee.
